name: Mars
lede: Mars is a warm orange named for the planet, one of a family of Mars pigments (Mars yellow, Mars red, Mars black) made from synthetic iron oxide rather than natural earths.

sections.title: An iron-oxide name
sections.body:
The library dates this orange to Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, first recorded in 1835, plate 11 L 9, with earlier alternate names Tron Yellow (1860) and Siderin Yellow also tied to the same plate [1]. The Mars pigments take their name from the alchemical sign for iron, which was also the sign for the planet and the god [1].

They were developed as a cheaper, more consistent substitute for natural ochres and siennas once chemists learned to precipitate synthetic iron oxide [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 files this value as a moderate brown [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[faded-orange]] and [[dull-orange]], at 2.7 and 3.1 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a color within six units of this one in 112, about 0.5 percent, as photographed [2]. The earliest is a 1415 panel by Martino di Bartolomeo, and it peaks in the 1500s, in 9 of 417 paintings, at 4.6 times the archive's overall rate [2]. It most often sits as a highlight rather than a shadow, and shares canvases with [[ochre|Ochre]] and [[sienna|Sienna]] more than chance would predict [2]. The match is a screen color, not proof of an actual iron-oxide pigment [2].
